title: Review 75: EAZ vs OA vs MAT-Led Reform
author: SMARTcurriculum Network
summary: This weekly review compares three decades of English attempts to intervene in disadvantaged areas: Education Action Zones (1998 to 2003), Opportunity Areas (2016 to 2022) and multi-academy trust led reform. It presents each as a different theory of change, with EAZs relying on local autonomy and experimentation, OAs on data-led targeting inside a bounded framework, and MATs on structural consolidation, scale and trust-level accountability. The paper weighs strengths and risks of each, concluding that EAZs were high on innovation but low on system coherence, OAs were more systemically literate but risked over-specification, and MATs offer scalability but may homogenise local context. It also compares funding, curriculum approach and outcomes, and draws five lessons: autonomy without capacity is insufficient, integration with system governance is crucial, data-driven targeting matters, leadership pipelines must be sustained, and strategies must balance standardisation with local adaptation. The closing line places the child's lived experience, not the system, at the centre.
points: The comparison frames three English reforms as three answers to the same question, namely how the system should intervene where it is weakest.
EAZs showed that local freedom without professional and organisational capacity produces pockets of promising practice that do not scale.
OAs combined multi-year funding, KPIs and wider ecosystem concerns such as early years and teacher retention, at the price of some local agency.
MATs embed financial planning, professional development pipelines and consistent curriculum progression, but outcomes depend heavily on trust leadership quality.
The shared lesson is that longevity and embedded system capacity matter more than short-term funding or autonomy alone.
quotes: What is striking over the past three decades of English education reform is not simply the persistence of place-based disadvantage, but the shifting theory of change underpinning government intervention.
EAZs were, therefore, high on innovation but low on system coherence. They generated pockets of promising practice, but struggled to translate these into scalable improvement.
Autonomy still existed, but it was bounded autonomy—flexibility within a framework of national expectations.
Improvement is achieved through scale, consistency, and professional alignment, rather than localised innovation.
MATs represent the most systemically embedded reform, but also the most removed from the original ethos of localised partnership seen in EAZs.
Key lesson: Longevity and embedded system capacity matter more than short-term funding or autonomy alone.
Autonomy is insufficient without capacity: EAZs showed local freedom is not enough.
